title: Review: Shapes of molecules (VSEPR); Stereoisomerism (E/Z and optical); Amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA; Giant covalent structures
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD05#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR25b#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD03#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD03#N.6, BD05#N.7, OR05#N.4b, OR25a#N.4, OR25b#N.14a, BD03#N.3b, BD05#N.11b, OR05#N.14b, OR25a#N.14c, BD03#N.5b, OR05#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Graphene
items.clue: A single sheet one atom thick that conducts and is very strong for its mass.

items.label: Enzyme
items.clue: A protein that acts as a catalyst: it speeds up a reaction and is not used up.

items.label: VSEPR
items.clue: Model in which electron pairs around a central atom get as far apart as possible.

items.label: Graphite
items.clue: Flat layers of hexagons that slide over each other, so it is soft, yet it conducts.

questions.stem: Which molecule has a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but a bent molecular geometry?

options.text: SO₂
CH₄
NH₃
H₂S

questions.explanation: S has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, like O in water: tetrahedral arrangement, and the atoms H–S–H are bent.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: cis-But-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene do not turn into each other at room temperature. Which statement best explains why?

options.text: Turning one end of the C=C would twist the p orbitals apart and break the pi bond, which needs much more energy than is available at room temperature.
Turning one end would break the sigma bond, which is the stronger of the two bonds.
The two CH₃ groups repel each other strongly, so they cannot pass each other.
They are the same compound drawn in two ways, so there is nothing to turn into.

questions.explanation: The pi bond comes from side-by-side overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis. Rotation destroys that overlap, so the two isomers are locked.

questions.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which species of glycine is present?

options.text: H₂NCH₂COOH₂⁺
⁺H₃NCH₂COOH
H₂NCH₂COO⁻
⁺H₃NCH₂COCl

questions.explanation: The –NH₂ base group accepts H⁺ from the acid. The –COOH stays un-ionised in excess acid.

questions.stem: An enzyme from the small intestine works best near pH 7. At pH 2 it stops working, although no covalent bonds in it break. Which explanation is best? (Hint: some side chains end in –COO⁻ at pH 7.)

options.text: H⁺ turns –COO⁻ side chains into –COOH; ionic attractions are lost and the active site changes shape.
The acid rapidly hydrolyses the peptide links, so the enzyme breaks apart into its separate amino acids.
H⁺ ions occupy the active site and are held there in place of the substrate molecules.
At pH 2 the substrate molecules move more slowly, so fewer of them collide with the enzyme.

questions.stem: Which pair of species have different molecular geometries?

options.text: NCl₃ and BCl₃
CO₂ and XeF₂
SO₂ and H₂O
BCl₃ and CO₃²⁻

questions.explanation: BCl₃: three bonding domains, no lone pair, trigonal planar. NCl₃: three bonds and a lone pair, tetrahedral domains, trigonal pyramidal.

questions.stem: Silicon carbide, SiC, is a covalent network solid. Every Si atom is bonded to four C atoms, and every C atom to four Si atoms, tetrahedrally, in three dimensions. Which pair of properties does this structure predict?

options.text: High melting point, but soft, because layers of atoms slide over one another easily.
Low melting point and soft, because weak intermolecular forces hold SiC molecules together.
High melting point and very hard, because strong covalent bonds at fixed angles run in 3D.
High melting point and malleable, because its atoms can rearrange without bonds breaking.

questions.stem: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene boils at about 60 °C; trans-1,2-dichloroethene boils at about 48 °C. Both are ClHC=CHCl. Which explains why they are two separate compounds with different boiling points?

options.text: Rotation about the C=C bond interconverts them, so the samples must differ in purity, not structure.
The C=C bond in the trans isomer is weaker, so less energy is needed to break it when it boils.
The cis isomer has more electrons, so its London dispersion forces are much stronger.
The pi bond blocks rotation, and only the cis isomer is polar, giving dipole–dipole forces.

questions.stem: In a folded protein, a side chain ending in –COOH and a side chain ending in –NH₂ sit next to each other. At the pH inside a cell, the first is –COO⁻ and the second is –NH₃⁺. Which statement best describes the interaction between them?

options.text: A covalent bond forms, because an acid and a base react to give a new compound.
Opposite charges attract noncovalently, helping hold the protein's shape.
Only London dispersion forces act, because both groups are in the same molecule.
A hydrogen bond forms between two H atoms, one on each side chain.

questions.explanation: The acid group has lost H⁺ and the base group gained it. The −1 and +1 groups attract: an ion–ion interaction in one molecule.

questions.stem: In CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O, the central atom is surrounded by four electron domains. According to VSEPR theory, how does the H–X–H bond angle (X = C, N or O) change from CH₄ to NH₃ to H₂O, and why?

options.text: It increases, as fewer bonded atoms around the central atom can spread farther apart
It increases, as bonding pairs repel each other more strongly than lone pairs repel them
It stays at 109.5°, as four electron domains give a tetrahedral molecular shape
It decreases, as lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other

questions.explanation: 0, 1, then 2 lone pairs. Each squeezes the angle: 109.5°, about 107°, about 104.5°.

questions.stem: Which compound can exist as cis and trans stereoisomers about its C=C bond?

options.text: CH₂=C(CH₃)₂
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃
CCl₂=CHCl
CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₂CH₃

questions.explanation: Each C=C carbon carries an H and a C₂H₅. Rotation is blocked, so the two arrangements are different compounds.
